name: Sports Psychology
description: An applied course exploring the psychological principles that influence athletic performance, including motivation, goal setting, mental imagery, team dynamics, and achieving peak performance states.

modules.title: Introduction to Sports Psychology
modules.objectives: Define sports psychology, identify its major research areas, and explain how mental skills training improves athletic performance. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Read the AASP field overview. Required course instruction: sport psychology examines thoughts, feelings and behavior in sport, including motivation, attention, anxiety, confidence and team interaction. Mental skills are learned preparation strategies, not substitutes for physical practice or medical care. Example: Avery records whether a task cue brings attention back before each timed lap. A useful research question compares this observable behavior across comparable practices; a faster lap alone cannot establish that the cue caused it.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Introduction to Sports Psychology. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.

Use the linked AASP article for one cited connection. Submit the assignment separately; no personal disclosure or actual exercise is required.
modules.assignment: Use this fictional case: Avery, a beginner swimmer, practices the same laps as a teammate but becomes distracted before a timed lap; the teammate uses a brief cue and a steady practice routine. In 250–350 words, distinguish physical practice from two mental factors, identify one sports-psychology research question, and propose one measurable mental skill Avery could try. Cite the module lesson and reading, explain what evidence would show improvement, and avoid claiming a guaranteed performance gain. Submit one document with your case analysis and a two-row evidence table. Evaluation: accurate concepts (40%), evidence and causal limits (35%), feasible measure and clear writing (25%). You may instead analyze a fictional sport of your choice; no personal health or performance disclosure is required. modules.title: Motivation in Sport
modules.objectives: Distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic motivation, apply Self-Determination Theory to athletic contexts, and identify strategies for building and sustaining motivation.
modules.readingNote: Read the AASP rewards article, then this required SDT lesson. Intrinsic motivation means doing an activity for its enjoyment or challenge; extrinsic motivation means doing it for a separable outcome, such as a prize. Self-Determination Theory identifies autonomy (volition and meaningful choice), competence (feeling effective and developing skill), and relatedness (feeling connected and respected). Example: let Jordan choose between two suitable drills (autonomy), give specific feedback on a developing pass (competence), and pair teammates for supportive practice (relatedness). Autonomy includes structure and safety. Controlling rewards can undermine intrinsic interest; informative feedback need not do so. Check engagement across several practices rather than assuming a guaranteed effect. Free supplementary theory overview: https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/theory/ .
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Motivation in Sport. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.

Use the linked AASP article for one cited connection. Submit the assignment separately; no personal disclosure or actual exercise is required.
modules.assignment: Use this fictional case: Jordan enjoys basketball practice but begins attending only for a promised prize; attendance drops when the prize ends. modules.title: Goal Setting
modules.objectives: Distinguish outcome, performance, and process goals; apply the SMART framework to sport goals; understand the role of goal tracking in athletic success. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Read AASP Principles of Effective Goal Setting with this correction: do not use its table's classification of improved free-throw percentage and fewer fouls as outcome goals. In this course these are performance standards. Outcome = competitive result relative to others (finish in the top three); performance = measured personal standard (raise free-throw accuracy from 60% to 65% across comparable 20-shot practices); process = execution behavior (use the same pre-shot cue before each attempt). Actions are more directly controllable than measured scores; even a personal time depends on conditions. SMART means specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Example: record cue use for 20 attempts at each of the next four practices and review the log weekly. A combined plan can link direction, benchmarks and actions; no combination is universally superior.

modules.title: Arousal, Anxiety & Stress
modules.objectives: Explain the Inverted-U Hypothesis and its application to sport performance, differentiate cognitive and somatic anxiety, and identify pre-competition anxiety management strategies.
modules.readingNote: Read the AASP anxiety article and this required model explanation. Arousal is activation or alertness, not necessarily anxiety. The inverted-U is a simplified hypothesis: performance may rise from under-arousal to a task- and person-specific optimum, then decline at excessive arousal. It is not a universal curve or a diagnostic rule. Cognitive anxiety involves worry; somatic anxiety involves bodily signs such as tense shoulders. Example: a player tries a comfortable breathing pause and a familiar task cue, then observes readiness across practices. Precision tasks may favor lower activation than forceful tasks, but individual responses vary. Do not diagnose from a heartbeat or force breath-holding; persistent distress belongs with a trusted adult or qualified professional.

modules.title: Attention & Concentration
modules.objectives: Understand attentional styles (broad/narrow, internal/external), identify concentration disruptions in sport, and practice attention control techniques. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Read the AASP cue-statements article and this required attention lesson. Width is broad (several cues) versus narrow (one cue); direction is external (environment) versus internal (thought or sensation). Broad-external: scan teammates and defenders. Narrow-external: attend to one passing target. Broad-internal: consider several possible plays mentally. Narrow-internal: silently repeat one cue or notice one breath. Useful focus changes with the moment; no style is always best. After an error, identify the current task and use a brief relevant cue instead of mentally replaying the error during live play.

modules.title: Mental Imagery & Visualization
modules.objectives: Define mental imagery in sport, explain PETTLEP imagery model components, and practice visualization scripts for performance enhancement. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Read AASP Sport Imagery Training and this required PETTLEP lesson. Imagery mentally rehearses a task using relevant sensory detail; it complements physical learning and does not guarantee improvement. PETTLEP is a task-matching checklist: Physical (appropriate posture and movement feel), Environment (familiar court), Task (the actual skill), Timing (realistic movement pace), Learning (current ability and updates as skill changes), Emotion (realistic feelings without forced distress), Perspective (first-person or observer viewpoint selected for the task). Example: imagine a seated, gentle ball pass, feeling the grip, seeing the target and rehearsing at normal speed from your own viewpoint. Observer imagery instead views the learner from outside. Motor imagery can recruit some overlapping movement-related brain systems; it is not identical to exercise. Sensory relevance matters more than adding every possible sense. Accessible peer-reviewed overview of the seven PETTLEP elements and evidence limits: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5351796/ .

modules.title: Self-Confidence & Self-Efficacy
modules.objectives: Differentiate self-confidence and self-efficacy, explain Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy, and develop strategies to build athletic confidence. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Read the AASP youth-motivation article and this required self-efficacy lesson. Self-confidence is broad confidence; self-efficacy is belief in ability to execute a particular task in a particular setting. Bandura's four sources are mastery (your successful task experience), vicarious experience (a similar learner models success), verbal persuasion (credible, specific encouragement), and interpretation of physiological/emotional states (how ordinary nerves are understood). Example: Morgan records successful serves, watches a similar peer, hears feedback tied to a demonstrated technique, and treats ordinary alertness as a preparation cue rather than proof of failure. Mastery provides direct evidence and is generally especially influential, not a guarantee. Task-specific belief can support effort and persistence; missing once does not define a person's ability or worth. Accessible sport-specific review of the four efficacy sources and their relationship to performance: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10675036/ .

modules.title: Team Cohesion & Leadership
modules.objectives: Define team cohesion and its two types (task and social), explain the leadership styles effective in sport settings, and identify strategies for building team unity.
modules.readingNote: Read the AASP team-culture article and this required leadership lesson. Task cohesion means coordinating toward shared performance goals; social cohesion means interpersonal connection and enjoyment. Friends can still have unclear match roles. Autocratic leadership concentrates decisions in the coach; democratic leadership invites athlete participation; transformational leadership develops shared purpose, models values and gives individualized support; transactional leadership relies on contingent exchanges such as rewards; servant leadership prioritizes members' development and needs. These categories can overlap in practice. Example: a coach invites role suggestions (democratic), then agrees a clear rotation and reviews coordination over three practices. A shared vision with individual support illustrates transformational coaching; no style is always best. A mastery climate emphasizes effort, learning and personal progress over public rankings.

quizQuestions.question: Sports psychology primarily focuses on:
options: Energy intake and nutrient requirements for athletes
The mental and psychological factors that influence athletic performance
Physical loading and cardiovascular conditioning
Muscle mechanics and joint forces during movement
quizQuestions.answer: The mental and psychological factors that influence athletic performance
quizQuestions.explanation: Sports psychology studies how psychological factors — motivation, confidence, anxiety, focus — affect sport performance and well-being.

quizQuestions.question: Which is an example of a mental skill used in sports psychology?
options: An aerobic conditioning session
A flexibility and mobility routine
Visualization and mental imagery
Progressive resistance training
quizQuestions.answer: Visualization and mental imagery
quizQuestions.explanation: Visualization (mental imagery) is a core mental skill in sports psychology, used to mentally rehearse performance before competition.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is NOT a typical focus area in sports psychology?
options: Motivation and goal setting in athletes
Team cohesion and leadership
Biomechanics of joint movement and muscle mechanics
Pre-competition anxiety management
quizQuestions.answer: Biomechanics of joint movement and muscle mechanics
quizQuestions.explanation: Biomechanics studies the physical mechanics of movement; sports psychology focuses on psychological factors — motivation, confidence, anxiety, and focus — that influence athletic performance.

quizQuestions.question: Name one mental skill an athlete could train and explain one observable way to check its use.
quizQuestions.answer: For example, concentration: record whether the athlete returns attention to the next play after a cue. Confidence, imagery, motivation or arousal regulation with a matching observation are acceptable.
quizQuestions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): name one relevant mental skill (0.5) and give a matching observable check (0.5). Partial credit: 0.5 for either element alone. Zero: neither element. Training does not guarantee a performance gain.

quizQuestions.question: Intrinsic motivation in sport refers to participating:
options: To avoid a penalty for missing practice
To gain approval from a respected coach
To earn a promised attendance prize
For the inherent enjoyment, challenge, and personal satisfaction of the activity
quizQuestions.answer: For the inherent enjoyment, challenge, and personal satisfaction of the activity
quizQuestions.explanation: Intrinsic motivation comes from within — the joy of the activity itself, personal challenge, and the satisfaction of improvement.

quizQuestions.question: Self-Determination Theory identifies which three basic psychological needs?
options: Autonomy, competence, and relatedness
Competence, recognition and security
Relatedness, achievement and control
Autonomy, status and relatedness
quizQuestions.answer: Autonomy, competence, and relatedness
quizQuestions.explanation: Self-Determination Theory (SDT) identifies autonomy, competence, and relatedness as the three fundamental psychological needs that fuel intrinsic motivation.

quizQuestions.question: A learner who enjoyed practice begins attending for a controlling prize and then loses interest when it ends. Which outcome illustrates the undermining effect?
options: The undermining effect — decreased intrinsic motivation
A shift from prize seeking to enjoyment of the activity itself
Interest that depends less on the reward over time
Stable enjoyment even after a controlling prize is removed
quizQuestions.answer: The undermining effect — decreased intrinsic motivation
quizQuestions.explanation: A controlling reward can shift attention away from enjoyment toward the prize, leaving less intrinsic interest when it ends. This is a possible risk, not a claim that every reward or learner shows the same effect.

quizQuestions.question: According to Self-Determination Theory, which coaching approach best supports athlete autonomy?
options: Basing every practice choice on a performance prize
Assigning one drill without discussing the athlete's perspective
Giving technical feedback without offering a meaningful choice
Providing rationale, meaningful choices, and acknowledgment of athletes' perspectives
quizQuestions.answer: Providing rationale, meaningful choices, and acknowledgment of athletes' perspectives
quizQuestions.explanation: Autonomy-supportive coaching satisfies the SDT need for autonomy by giving athletes reasons for tasks, offering choices, and valuing their input — in contrast to controlling behavior.

quizQuestions.question: Which type of goal focuses on the end result (winning or placing)?
options: Process goal
Performance goal
Participation goal
Outcome goal
quizQuestions.answer: Outcome goal
quizQuestions.explanation: Outcome goals focus on end results like winning a competition or ranking, which are partially outside the athlete's control.

quizQuestions.question: In goal setting, a process goal focuses on:
options: Achieving a personal accuracy percentage
The specific behaviors and actions within performance (e.g., 'keep hips forward')
Finishing in the top three
Beating a specific opponent
quizQuestions.answer: The specific behaviors and actions within performance (e.g., 'keep hips forward')
quizQuestions.explanation: Process goals focus on technical execution — specific actions and behaviors the athlete performs during competition.

quizQuestions.question: Which sequence lists an outcome goal, a performance goal and a process goal, in that order?
options: Place in the top three; reach a personal accuracy target; use a pre-shot cue
Use a cue; place in the top three; reach a personal accuracy target
Reach a personal accuracy target; use a cue; place in the top three
Place in the top three; use a cue; reach a personal accuracy target
quizQuestions.answer: Place in the top three; reach a personal accuracy target; use a pre-shot cue
quizQuestions.explanation: Outcome goals compare competitive results, performance goals set personal measures, and process goals specify execution. Linking them organizes a plan without proving that this combination is always most effective.

quizQuestions.question: Give one measurable performance goal for a fictional swimmer and contrast it with a process goal.
quizQuestions.answer: Performance: reduce a 50-metre practice time from 50 to 49 seconds within six weeks under comparable conditions. Process: use the agreed turn cue at each turn. Equivalent measured personal standards and specific execution cues are acceptable.
quizQuestions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): a measurable personal standard rather than competitive placing (0.5), plus a specific execution/process contrast (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either correct element. Zero: neither. A measured time is influenced by conditions and is less directly controllable than cue use.

quizQuestions.question: In the simplified inverted-U model, which arousal-performance pattern is predicted?
options: Performance rises toward an optimum, then falls as arousal rises further
Performance remains unchanged as arousal rises
Performance falls at a constant rate as arousal rises
Performance rises at a constant rate as arousal rises
quizQuestions.answer: Performance rises toward an optimum, then falls as arousal rises further
quizQuestions.explanation: The model proposes a curved relationship, not an indefinitely rising line. The optimum and actual pattern vary by task and athlete; the curve is a teaching hypothesis.

quizQuestions.question: Cognitive anxiety in sport refers to:
options: Sweaty palms during a pre-shot routine
An elevated heartbeat noticed before a start
Physical muscle tension before competition
Mental worry and negative thoughts about performance
quizQuestions.answer: Mental worry and negative thoughts about performance
quizQuestions.explanation: Cognitive anxiety involves negative thoughts, worry, and fear of failure — the mental component of pre-competition anxiety.

quizQuestions.question: In Arousal, Anxiety & Stress, Somatic anxiety refers to:
options: A belief that teammates will judge a mistake
Physical symptoms of anxiety such as increased heart rate, sweating, and muscle tension
Worry about making the next shot
Mental rehearsal of possible failure
quizQuestions.answer: Physical symptoms of anxiety such as increased heart rate, sweating, and muscle tension
quizQuestions.explanation: Somatic anxiety involves the physical symptoms of nervous arousal — elevated heart rate, sweating, nausea, and muscle tension.

quizQuestions.question: What is an intended use of a comfortable, slow breathing routine before performance?
options: Raise activation before an explosive effort
Shift attention outward to scan several defenders
Help regulate arousal when the athlete feels overactivated
Increase range of motion in a warm-up
quizQuestions.answer: Help regulate arousal when the athlete feels overactivated
quizQuestions.explanation: A comfortable breathing pause may help a learner regulate activation. Responses vary: it does not establish a universal optimum or replace preparation. Do not force deep breathing, breath-holding or practice that causes discomfort.

quizQuestions.question: Which attentional focus is described as 'broad-external'?
options: Scanning the field to read the environment and other players
Mentally weighing several tactical options
Attending to a single internal breath
Attending to one outside target
quizQuestions.answer: Scanning the field to read the environment and other players
quizQuestions.explanation: Broad-external attention involves scanning the environment broadly — reading the field, tracking multiple players, and assessing the situation.

quizQuestions.question: A player silently compares several possible tactical plans before the next play. Which attentional style is illustrated?
options: Narrow-external
Broad-internal
Broad-external
Narrow-internal
quizQuestions.answer: Broad-internal
quizQuestions.explanation: Considering several alternatives makes the focus broad; evaluating them mentally makes it internal. Scanning several players would instead be broad-external.

quizQuestions.question: Narrow-internal attentional focus in sport involves:
options: Scanning several teammates and defenders
Focusing on one internal sensation, such as a single breath
Attending to a single external passing target
Mentally comparing several tactical options
quizQuestions.answer: Focusing on one internal sensation, such as a single breath
quizQuestions.explanation: Narrow concerns one selected cue; internal concerns a thought or bodily sensation. Considering several plans is broad-internal, and watching a target is narrow-external.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is an example of a concentration disruption during sport performance?
options: Using a pre-performance cue word to refocus
Scanning the field for open teammates
Dwelling on a previous error while the next play is live
Using controlled breathing before a free throw
quizQuestions.answer: Dwelling on a previous error while the next play is live
quizQuestions.explanation: Ruminating about a past mistake is a common concentration disruption — it diverts attention from the current performance moment to an irrelevant past event.

quizQuestions.question: Which description illustrates task-relevant multisensory imagery?
options: Watching a recording without mentally rehearsing the skill
Picturing the scoreboard without rehearsing the movement
Imagining the target, the feel of the ball and familiar court sounds
Writing a result target without imagining the task
quizQuestions.answer: Imagining the target, the feel of the ball and familiar court sounds
quizQuestions.explanation: Imagery can include relevant sights, sounds and movement sensations. This describes a rehearsal method; it does not establish a statistically superior effect for every learner.

quizQuestions.question: Internal imagery perspective means:
options: Describing a movement without mentally experiencing it
Imagining the performance from your own viewpoint — as if inside your body
Watching yourself from an outside observer's viewpoint
Viewing a recording without mentally rehearsing the movement
quizQuestions.answer: Imagining the performance from your own viewpoint — as if inside your body
quizQuestions.explanation: Internal imagery places the athlete 'inside' their body, experiencing the kinesthetic feel of the movement during visualization.

quizQuestions.question: Which account of motor imagery is consistent with partial overlap in movement-related brain activity?
options: It operates through visual processing without movement representation
It duplicates the physical training load of the movement
It recruits movement systems identical in every respect to execution
Imagined and executed movement can recruit some overlapping brain systems
quizQuestions.answer: Imagined and executed movement can recruit some overlapping brain systems
quizQuestions.explanation: Imagery can involve movement-related representation also used in execution. Partial overlap does not mean identical activation, equal physical loading or a guaranteed training effect.

quizQuestions.question: A learner updates an imagery script after learning a new passing technique. Which PETTLEP element is most directly illustrated?
options: Learning
Perspective
Environment
Timing
quizQuestions.answer: Learning
quizQuestions.explanation: Learning means adapting the script to current skill and updating it as technique develops. Timing concerns pace; environment concerns setting; perspective concerns viewpoint.

quizQuestions.question: Describe one appropriate use of imagery and one limit of that use.
quizQuestions.answer: A fictional learner mentally rehearses a familiar passing routine before practice; the rehearsal complements instruction and physical practice rather than guaranteeing success. Other safe, task-matched examples are acceptable.
quizQuestions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): a concrete task-relevant imagery use (0.5) and an appropriate limit such as no guaranteed gain or no replacement of physical learning (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for one element. Zero: neither.

quizQuestions.question: Self-efficacy, as defined by Bandura, refers to:
options: A comparison of one's social standing with teammates
Belief in one's ability to perform a specific task successfully
A broad feeling of confidence across life situations
A general judgment of one's personal worth
quizQuestions.answer: Belief in one's ability to perform a specific task successfully
quizQuestions.explanation: Self-efficacy is situation-specific confidence — the belief that you can execute a specific behavior or skill successfully.

quizQuestions.question: In Bandura's framework, which source generally provides the most direct evidence of capability?
options: Watching others perform successfully
Physiological arousal
Verbal encouragement from others
Mastery experiences (past successes)
quizQuestions.answer: Mastery experiences (past successes)
quizQuestions.explanation: Mastery experiences use one's own successful task performance as direct evidence. Modeling, persuasion and interpretation of arousal are other sources; their effects depend on the person and context.

quizQuestions.question: Vicarious experience as a source of self-efficacy in sport means:
options: Receiving specific encouragement from a coach
Reviewing one's own successful serving attempts
Observing a similar-ability peer succeed at the same task
Interpreting one's ordinary pre-shot alertness
quizQuestions.answer: Observing a similar-ability peer succeed at the same task
quizQuestions.explanation: Vicarious experience (modeling) raises self-efficacy by showing that someone of similar ability can accomplish the task — strengthening the observer's belief that they can do it too.

quizQuestions.question: How can task-specific self-efficacy influence an athlete's response to a setback? Give one observable behavior.
quizQuestions.answer: Belief in being able to execute a particular skill can support persistence; for example, Morgan attempts the next manageable serving drill after an error. Equivalent task-specific examples are acceptable.
quizQuestions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): connect belief about a specific task to a response (0.5), and give an observable behavior such as returning to a suitable drill (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. High efficacy does not guarantee success or justify ignoring safety.

quizQuestions.question: Task cohesion in a sport team refers to:
options: The extent to which teammates enjoy social time together
The degree of confidence each athlete feels in a particular skill
The amount of decision authority held by the coach
The degree to which team members work together to achieve team goals
quizQuestions.answer: The degree to which team members work together to achieve team goals
quizQuestions.explanation: Task cohesion reflects how well team members cooperate and coordinate to achieve shared performance objectives.

quizQuestions.question: Which leadership style involves the leader making all decisions without athlete input?
options: Autocratic
Transformational
Servant
Democratic
quizQuestions.answer: Autocratic
quizQuestions.explanation: Autocratic leadership involves the coach making all decisions without seeking or considering input from athletes.

quizQuestions.question: Transformational leadership in sport is characterized by:
options: Inviting athletes to vote on a practice decision
Inspiring athletes through vision, individual consideration, and motivating beyond self-interest
Centralizing tactical decisions in the coach
Using contingent rewards to exchange effort for incentives
quizQuestions.answer: Inspiring athletes through vision, individual consideration, and motivating beyond self-interest
quizQuestions.explanation: Transformational coaches inspire athletes with a shared vision, individualize support, and motivate intrinsic values beyond external rewards.

quizQuestions.question: Social cohesion in a sport team refers to:
options: Agreement about technical responsibilities
Confidence in executing a specific skill
The degree to which athletes like each other and enjoy being together as a group
Coordination toward shared match objectives
quizQuestions.answer: The degree to which athletes like each other and enjoy being together as a group
quizQuestions.explanation: Social cohesion reflects the interpersonal bonds and friendships among team members, whereas task cohesion describes coordinated effort toward shared performance objectives.

questions.question: Sports psychology primarily studies which aspect of athletic performance?
options: Nutrition for competition
Psychological and mental factors affecting sport performance
Physical conditioning techniques
Biomechanics of movement
questions.answer: Psychological and mental factors affecting sport performance
questions.explanation: Sports psychology focuses on mental and psychological factors — motivation, anxiety, confidence, focus — that affect athletic performance.

questions.question: Intrinsic motivation in sport comes from:
options: Coach approval and team pressure
Internal enjoyment, challenge, and personal satisfaction
External rewards like trophies or money
Fear of failure
questions.answer: Internal enjoyment, challenge, and personal satisfaction
questions.explanation: Intrinsic motivation is driven by personal enjoyment, curiosity, and the inherent satisfaction of the activity itself.

questions.question: Which three needs does Self-Determination Theory connect to intrinsic motivation?
options: Competence, recognition and security
Relatedness, achievement and control
Autonomy, status and relatedness
Autonomy, competence, and relatedness
questions.answer: Autonomy, competence, and relatedness
questions.explanation: SDT identifies autonomy, competence, and relatedness as the three psychological needs that fuel intrinsic motivation.

questions.question: Which type of goal focuses on controllable behaviors during performance?
options: Performance goals
Process goals
Participation goals
Outcome goals
questions.answer: Process goals
questions.explanation: Process goals specify execution behavior, such as using a pre-shot cue. A performance goal specifies a personal standard; an outcome goal specifies competitive placing.

questions.question: In the simplified inverted-U hypothesis, where is performance predicted to peak?
options: At every arousal level equally
At the lowest measurable arousal level
At the highest measurable arousal level
At an intermediate, task- and person-dependent arousal level
questions.answer: At an intermediate, task- and person-dependent arousal level
questions.explanation: The model predicts an optimum between under- and over-arousal. It does not prescribe the same activation level for every athlete or task.

questions.question: Cognitive anxiety refers to:
options: Negative thoughts and mental worry about performance
High energy and excitement
Optimal readiness for competition
Physical symptoms like nausea
questions.answer: Negative thoughts and mental worry about performance
questions.explanation: Cognitive anxiety involves mental worry, negative self-talk, and fear of failure — the psychological component of pre-competition anxiety.

questions.question: Describe internal imagery perspective and contrast it with an observer perspective.
questions.answer: Internal imagery rehearses from the learner's own first-person viewpoint. Observer imagery views the learner from outside, as if watching a recording.
questions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): first-person viewpoint (0.5) and an accurate outside-view contrast (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. Equivalent wording is acceptable; listing every sense is not required.

questions.question: In Bandura's framework, which source generally provides the most direct evidence of capability?
options: Verbal encouragement grounded in a coach's assessment
Interpretation of one's physiological and emotional state
Mastery experiences or successful performance accomplishments
Vicarious experience from a similar learner's success
questions.answer: Mastery experiences or successful performance accomplishments
questions.explanation: Mastery experiences use one's own successful task performance as direct evidence. Modeling, persuasion and interpretation of arousal are other sources; their effects depend on the person and context.

questions.question: In team sport, what does task cohesion describe?
options: Team members working together toward shared performance goals
Enjoying one another's company away from matches
Giving the coach control of tactical decisions
Believing personally that one can execute a particular skill
questions.answer: Team members working together toward shared performance goals
questions.explanation: Task cohesion reflects the degree to which team members coordinate and cooperate to achieve their shared competitive objectives.

questions.question: A 'cue word' in concentration training is used to:
options: Provide a detailed technical explanation during a rapid action
Evaluate the final competitive result against an opponent
Compare several past mistakes during live play
Rapidly redirect attention to a key performance element
questions.answer: Rapidly redirect attention to a key performance element
questions.explanation: Cue words serve as mental triggers that quickly refocus an athlete's attention on a critical performance aspect.

questions.question: Which is the best example of an outcome goal for a high school basketball player?
options: Use the agreed pre-shot cue on every attempt
Increase free-throw accuracy to 80%
Win the state championship
Complete the planned ball-handling drill each practice
questions.answer: Win the state championship
questions.explanation: Winning the state championship is an outcome goal focused on the competitive result, partly outside the athlete's direct control.

questions.question: Broad-external attentional focus is most useful for which sport situation?
options: Attending to a single breath before the next action
Scanning the field or court to read teammates, opponents, and space
Mentally evaluating several possible tactical plans
Attending to one outside target before release
questions.answer: Scanning the field or court to read teammates, opponents, and space
questions.explanation: Broad-external focus processes several environmental cues. Monitoring one breath is narrow-internal, considering several plans is broad-internal, and watching one target is narrow-external.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes movement-related brain activity during motor imagery?
options: Some movement-related brain systems can overlap with those used in execution
Movement pathways only when the skill is physically executed
Visual pathways without any movement-related activity
Movement-related pathways identical in every respect to execution
questions.answer: Some movement-related brain systems can overlap with those used in execution
questions.explanation: Overlap helps explain why task-specific mental rehearsal is studied as a learning aid. Imagery is not identical to execution and does not supply its physical conditioning load.

questions.question: Using the simplified arousal model, describe a suitable activation level for a precision task and explain one limit of that prediction.
questions.answer: Relatively low-to-moderate activation may support calm, alert precision. The useful level varies by athlete and task, so the model does not specify a universal optimum.
questions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): calm but alert or relatively low-to-moderate activation (0.5) and person/task variation or the model's simplified status (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither; complete inactivity is not the target.

questions.question: Self-Determination Theory's concept of 'competence' in sport means:
options: Holding higher social status than teammates
Feeling connected and respected by the team
Feeling effective and capable in one's sport activities
Being given meaningful choice in practice
questions.answer: Feeling effective and capable in one's sport activities
questions.explanation: Competence need satisfaction involves feeling capable, effective, and growing in one's athletic skills — not necessarily winning.

questions.question: A beginner wants to study whether a cue improves focus. Which observation best matches this mental-skills question?
options: Compare lap times from practices held under different conditions
Record only the final league ranking after the season
Record a single post-match impression without noting cue use
Record cue use and attention to the next task over comparable practices
questions.answer: Record cue use and attention to the next task over comparable practices
questions.explanation: Repeated cue and attention records address the proposed mental skill. Competitive results alone have many causes and cannot isolate the cue effect.

questions.question: Which imagery plan follows PETTLEP for a familiar gentle ball pass?
options: Rehearse the final score without representing the passing task
Rehearse the familiar technique at an unrelated movement pace
Rehearse an advanced unfamiliar technique at realistic speed
Rehearse the current technique at realistic speed in a familiar setting
questions.answer: Rehearse the current technique at realistic speed in a familiar setting
questions.explanation: Task, learning, timing and environment should match what is being learned. Imagery supports preparation rather than replacing instruction or physical practice.

questions.question: A coach offers two suitable practice drills and explains their purpose. Which SDT need is most directly supported?
options: Competence
Autonomy
Competitive status
Relatedness
questions.answer: Autonomy
questions.explanation: Meaningful choice and a rationale support volition. Competence concerns effectiveness and relatedness concerns connection; the example emphasizes choice.

questions.question: A runner logs completion of a task cue and a personal time. Which statement best distinguishes these measures?
options: Cue use is a process measure; personal time is a performance measure
Cue use is an outcome measure; personal time is a process measure
Both are outcome measures because numbers are recorded
Cue use is a performance measure; personal time is an outcome measure
questions.answer: Cue use is a process measure; personal time is a performance measure
questions.explanation: A process measure records execution behavior. A personal time records a standard of performance, while an outcome goal concerns competitive placing.

questions.question: A player scans several defenders, then attends to one passing target. What attention shift occurs?
options: Narrow-internal to broad-external
Broad-internal to narrow-internal
Narrow-external to broad-internal
Broad-external to narrow-external
questions.answer: Broad-external to narrow-external
questions.explanation: Both phases concern outside information, so both are external. The shift from several cues to one changes width from broad to narrow.

questions.question: Give two features of transformational coaching, with a concrete example of one.
questions.answer: A coach develops shared purpose and gives individualized support; for example, the team agrees a coordination goal while the coach adapts feedback to each learner. Modeling values or encouraging thoughtful improvement are acceptable alternatives.
questions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): two accurate features (0.25 each) plus a specific matching example (0.5). Partial: add the earned components, up to 0.75 if incomplete. Zero: no accurate component. Rewards alone do not establish transformational coaching.

questions.question: A player reports worry about missing and tense shoulders. Which distinction is accurate?
options: Both describe cognitive anxiety rather than bodily signs
Worry is cognitive anxiety; shoulder tension is a somatic sign
Both describe bodily activation rather than cognitive worry
Worry is somatic anxiety; shoulder tension is a cognitive sign
questions.answer: Worry is cognitive anxiety; shoulder tension is a somatic sign
questions.explanation: Cognitive and somatic describe mental and bodily aspects respectively. These observations do not establish a diagnosis or the cause of performance.

questions.question: A mastery coaching climate emphasizes:
options: Personal improvement and effort over competitive outcome
Allocating praise primarily by comparison with teammates
Ranking athletes primarily by match results
Linking recognition primarily to external awards
questions.answer: Personal improvement and effort over competitive outcome
questions.explanation: Mastery climates promote intrinsic motivation by valuing personal growth, effort, and skill development over social comparison and winning.

questions.question: Why is a pre-performance routine valuable for athletes?
options: It makes imagery identical to physical rehearsal
It turns a personal accuracy target into an outcome goal
It supports consistent focus, arousal regulation, and readiness before performance
It establishes the same ideal arousal level for every athlete
questions.answer: It supports consistent focus, arousal regulation, and readiness before performance
questions.explanation: A routine helps athletes prepare attention and emotion; it does not replace physical preparation.

questions.question: Which check best evaluates a proposed concentration-reset routine?
options: Observe whether the player returns attention to the current task across practices
Use a single winning result as proof of the routine's effect
Use a general confidence rating without observing attention
Use practice duration as a substitute for observing cue use
questions.answer: Observe whether the player returns attention to the current task across practices
questions.explanation: A measure should match the routine's intended attention target. Repeated observations can inform revision but do not by themselves prove causation.

questions.question: After one missed serve, Morgan says they cannot serve under pressure. Which coaching response uses mastery evidence?
options: Discuss how Morgan interprets ordinary pre-shot alertness
Review recent successful serves in comparable practice and set a manageable next task
Ask Morgan to watch a similar peer complete a serve
Give Morgan credible encouragement about the next attempt
questions.answer: Review recent successful serves in comparable practice and set a manageable next task
questions.explanation: Mastery uses the learner's own successful performance. Peer modeling is vicarious experience and encouragement is persuasion; neither is the same source.

questions.question: Which verbal-persuasion source gives the learner the most relevant basis for a realistic task belief?
options: A comparison with an unrelated elite athlete
Credible, knowledgeable sources like coaches and experienced athletes
Encouragement promising a result regardless of preparation
Vague praise from someone who has not observed the skill
questions.answer: Credible, knowledgeable sources like coaches and experienced athletes
questions.explanation: Credible, knowledgeable feedback tied to observed skill can support realistic self-efficacy. It does not replace mastery evidence or justify a promise of success.

questions.question: A team socializes comfortably but players dispute match roles. Identify the weaker cohesion type and propose an observable step.
questions.answer: Task cohesion is weaker despite social cohesion. Agree role responsibilities and record whether players follow the rotation in the next three practices. Equivalent role-clarity measures are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): identify task cohesion (0.5), and propose a concrete coordination step with an observable check (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. Friendship does not establish coordinated performance.

questions.question: The PETTLEP imagery model stands for Physical, Environment, Task, Timing, Learning, Emotion, and:
options: Perspective
Performance
Practice
Power
questions.answer: Perspective
questions.explanation: PETTLEP = Physical, Environment, Task, Timing, Learning, Emotion, Perspective — a comprehensive framework for functional athletic imagery.

questions.question: A Personal Mental Performance Plan combines which key mental skills?
options: A tactical playbook, equipment checklist and travel schedule
An exercise-loading schedule, nutrition targets and sleep totals
Goal setting, imagery, concentration, arousal control, and confidence strategies
Competitive rankings, selection decisions and awards
questions.answer: Goal setting, imagery, concentration, arousal control, and confidence strategies
questions.explanation: A comprehensive mental performance plan integrates multiple psychological skills — goals, imagery, focus, arousal regulation, and confidence — customized for the individual.

questions.question: A coach silently considers several possible tactical plans. Which attentional style does this illustrate?
options: Broad-external
Narrow-internal
Broad-internal
Narrow-external
questions.answer: Broad-internal
questions.explanation: Several alternatives make the focus broad; mental planning makes it internal. Scanning several players would be broad-external instead.

questions.question: Autonomy support in sport means coaches do what?
options: Let the captain decide without consulting the other athletes
Assign drills and explain technique without inviting input
Offer a prize as the basis for every practice decision
Offer meaningful choices, rationale, and athlete input when appropriate
questions.answer: Offer meaningful choices, rationale, and athlete input when appropriate
questions.explanation: Autonomy-supportive coaching helps athletes feel ownership while still providing structure.

questions.question: Which feedback most directly supports competence without promising success?
options: You will earn a prize only if you beat the captain
Choose any drill; we will not discuss skill progress
Your passing cue was consistent on four attempts; use it again and review the next set
You are the best player, so you should win the next match
questions.answer: Your passing cue was consistent on four attempts; use it again and review the next set
questions.explanation: Specific feedback connects a demonstrated action to a next step. It gives information about effectiveness without a guaranteed result; there is no universal feedback formula.

questions.question: Which coaching practice best supports social cohesion in a team?
options: Comparing individual conditioning measures
Clarifying tactical responsibilities for the next rotation
Promoting team rituals, shared goals, and opportunities for athletes to bond
Setting a target for the team's passing accuracy
questions.answer: Promoting team rituals, shared goals, and opportunities for athletes to bond
questions.explanation: Social cohesion is built through shared experiences, team rituals, mutual support, and deliberate relationship-building opportunities.

questions.question: After a mistake during live play, propose an attention-reset action and explain why it fits the next task.
questions.answer: Use a brief cue such as target, then attend to the open teammate for the next pass. It redirects attention from the previous mistake to currently relevant information. Equivalent safe, specific routines are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Full credit (1 point): a specific reset action (0.5) and a link to current task information rather than the past error (0.5). Partial: 0.5 for either. Zero: neither. A reset does not guarantee the next play succeeds.
